I've been farming these same fields in Quzhou for over fifty years, and at seventy-four I don't have the back or the patience to gamble on newfangled crops. I keep six mu of flat land, and I'm sticking to the wheat–maize double crop because it feeds my family and puts a little cash in my pocket — it's the only system I trust. For the winter wheat, I'll sow an improved variety around the tenth of October. The extension fellow says fifteen kilograms of nitrogen per mu is plenty, but I learned the hard way that if the wheat turns yellow at jointing you spend the whole summer kicking yourself, so I always put down about sixteen kilograms of nitrogen, plus seven kilograms of phosphorus and five kilograms of potassium from compound fertilizer and a top-dressing of urea. I'll irrigate four times — before winter, at green-up, at jointing, and once at grain filling if the skies stay dry — and I'll spray three times for weeds, insects, and fungus. I rotary till before wheat because I like the stubble buried clean before the cold sets in.

For the summer maize, I'll plant hybrid seed the same week I cut the wheat in early June; the window is so tight there's no time for ploughing, so I switched to no-tillage a few years back after my nephew showed me it saved diesel and a day's hard labor without hurting the yield. Maize is less fussy — I give it fourteen kilograms of nitrogen and about three kilograms each of phosphorus and potassium per mu, irrigate twice, and spray pesticides two or three times depending on whether the corn borers show up. I expect around four hundred and eighty kilograms per mu of wheat and five hundred and twenty kilograms per mu of maize. Those aren't the biggest yields in the village, but they're steady, and at my age steady keeps the roof over my head.
